stem: A melodic interval is played once, lower note first. Which interval is heard?
rationale: C4 rises to B4, eleven semitones: an ascending major seventh, one half step short of the octave. A minor seventh spans ten semitones, a major sixth nine, and an octave twelve.

stem: Listen to the melodic interval, which moves from the higher pitch to the lower pitch. Which interval is heard?
rationale: E5 descends to G-sharp4, eight semitones: a descending minor sixth. A perfect fifth spans seven semitones, a major sixth nine, and an augmented fourth six.

stem: Two pitches are heard in succession, the second higher than the first. Which interval do they form?
rationale: F4 to B4 spans six semitones, the tritone (augmented fourth), which divides the octave in half and sounds unstable. A perfect fourth spans five semitones, a perfect fifth seven, and a minor sixth eight.

stem: Listen to the short melody. Which melodic device is most prominent?
rationale: A four-note motive (G–A–B–G) is restated beginning one step lower twice (F–G–A–F, then E–F–G–E) with the same rhythm: a descending diatonic sequence. Inversion would flip the contour, retrograde would reverse the note order, and augmentation would lengthen the durations.

stem: The excerpt ascends through a scale that begins and ends on F. Which mode is heard?
rationale: F–G–A–B–C–D–E–F is a major scale with a raised fourth degree (B-natural instead of B-flat): F Lydian. F Ionian contains B-flat, F Mixolydian contains B-flat and E-flat, and F Dorian contains A-flat, B-flat, and E-flat.

stem: Which pitch collection is heard in this ascending scale?
rationale: C–D–E–F-sharp–G-sharp–A-sharp–C contains six pitches separated only by whole steps, the whole-tone scale; it has no perfect fifth above the starting pitch. Major pentatonic includes minor thirds, Lydian includes half steps, and the chromatic scale moves entirely by half steps.

stem: Listen to the ascending scale from C to C. Which scale type is heard?
rationale: C–D-flat–E-flat–E–F-sharp–G–A–B-flat–C alternates half and whole steps and contains eight distinct pitches: the octatonic (diminished) scale. Harmonic minor and Phrygian have seven pitches, and the whole-tone scale has only whole steps.

stem: A three-note chord is played as an arpeggio and then as a simultaneous sonority. Which chord quality is heard?
rationale: C–E–G-sharp stacks two major thirds, producing an augmented triad with an augmented fifth above the root. A major triad has a perfect fifth (G), a minor triad has a minor third and perfect fifth, and a diminished triad stacks two minor thirds.

stem: A seventh chord is arpeggiated from the root and then sounded together. Which quality is heard?
rationale: F–A–C–E is a major triad with a major seventh above the root, a half step below the octave. A dominant seventh would have E-flat, a minor seventh A-flat and E-flat, and a minor-major seventh A-flat with E-natural.

stem: Which seventh-chord quality matches the chord heard first in broken form and then as a block?
rationale: B–D–F–A-flat stacks three minor thirds; its seventh is diminished. A half-diminished seventh would have A-natural, while dominant and minor sevenths are built on major or minor triads rather than a diminished triad.

stem: After a C-major introduction and a pause, listen to the final two chords, especially the highest voice. Which cadence is heard?
rationale: The ending moves from a root-position G-major dominant to a root-position C-major tonic, but the top voice ends on E, the third of the chord. V–I without the tonic in the soprano is an imperfect authentic cadence. A perfect authentic cadence would end with C on top, a half cadence would stop on V, and a plagal cadence would be IV–I.

stem: Following a C-major introduction and a pause, which cadence closes the final phrase?
rationale: The closing chords are F major (IV) moving to C major (I), the plagal or "Amen" progression. An authentic cadence approaches I from V, a half cadence ends on V, and a deceptive cadence moves from V to a chord other than I, usually vi.

stem: After an A-minor introduction and a pause, which cadence ends the excerpt?
rationale: The phrase ends on the dominant (E major) approached from iv6 (D minor with F in the bass), so the bass descends by half step F–E while the upper voice rises D–E. That iv6–V ending in minor is a Phrygian half cadence. The other cadences end on i or VI, not V.

stem: Listen to the two-voice excerpt. Which texture is heard?
rationale: A melody begins alone and the same melody enters an octave lower four notes later, so two independent lines overlap in strict imitation (a canon). Monophony has one line, homophony places one melody over supporting chords, and heterophony presents simultaneous variants of a single melody rather than a delayed entrance.

stem: The highest tones mark each downbeat, middle tones mark the other beats, and the lowest tones mark subdivisions. Which meter signature best fits?
rationale: Each measure contains three beats, and each beat divides into three equal subdivisions (nine per measure): compound triple, conventionally 9/8. 3/4 divides each beat in two, 6/8 has two dotted-quarter beats, and 12/8 has four.

stem: Listen to the accent pattern, in which the downbeat is highest, other beats are in the middle, and subdivisions are lowest. Which meter is most consistent?
rationale: Each measure has two beats, each divided into two equal parts: simple duple, conventionally 2/4. 6/8 would divide each of two beats into three, 3/4 would have three beats, and 5/8 would group an unequal 3+2 or 2+3.

stem: Listen to the repeating accent pattern. Which meter best describes the grouping of the equal subdivisions?
rationale: Each measure contains five equal subdivisions grouped as a long beat of three followed by a short beat of two, an asymmetrical 5/8. The other meters contain beats of equal length.

stem: A passage in triple meter temporarily shifts its accents before the original grouping returns. Which rhythmic device is heard?
rationale: After two measures accented in groups of three quarter notes, the next six quarter notes are accented in three groups of two, briefly implying a larger triple meter (3/2) across two bars of 3/4. That regrouping is hemiola. Rubato is flexible tempo, augmentation lengthens note values, and ostinato is a persistent repeated figure.

stem: Which tempo change occurs during the repeated-note excerpt?
rationale: The pitch and loudness stay the same while the time between attacks shrinks steadily, so the tempo gradually speeds up: accelerando. Ritardando slows down, a tempo restores a previous tempo, and a fermata holds one note beyond its value.

stem: Listen to the end of the descending phrase. Which change in tempo is heard?
rationale: The time between successive notes grows steadily longer as the phrase descends, a gradual slowing: ritardando. Accelerando would shorten the gaps, a fermata would sustain only one note, and a tempo signals a return to an earlier tempo rather than a gradual change.

stem: Listen to the repeated arpeggio figure. Which expressive change is heard?
distractors: a change from staccato to legato
rationale: The figure keeps the same pitches, tempo, and note lengths while each note is softer than the one before, a diminuendo. A crescendo would grow louder, a ritardando would slow down, and a legato change would lengthen notes.

stem: A short phrase is played four times in succession. Which dynamic practice is illustrated?
rationale: Each statement stays at one level and the next jumps abruptly: loud, soft, loud, soft. Block contrasts of this kind (echo effects) are terraced dynamics, typical of Baroque practice. Crescendo and diminuendo change gradually, and a sforzando is a single sudden accent.

stem: Listen to the ornament that decorates the second note of the melody. Which embellishment is heard?
rationale: The ornament is a quick four-note figure circling the main note: upper neighbor, main note, lower neighbor, main note (B–A–G-sharp–A). That is a turn. A trill alternates repeatedly with the upper neighbor, a mordent is a single quick alternation (main–neighbor–main), and a glissando slides continuously between pitches.

stem: Which embellishment is heard on the note that precedes the final resolution?
rationale: Before the melody resolves to C, the D is ornamented by rapid, repeated alternation with its upper neighbor E: a cadential trill. A turn is a single four-note figure, an appoggiatura is an accented dissonance resolving by step, and a mordent alternates only once.
